questions.stem: The straight line segment drawn across the circle shown (joining two points on the circle, NOT through the centre) is called a:

steps.explain: A chord is any straight line segment joining two points on the circle. A diameter is a special chord that passes through the centre.
steps.work: \text{The line does NOT pass through the centre} \implies \text{chord}

steps.explain: Pitfall: calling every straight line inside a circle a "diameter" (option B) — only chords through the centre are diameters. A radius (option C) joins the centre to the circle, and a tangent (option D) touches the circle from outside.

meta.sourcePaper: Hornsby Girls HS — Year 7 Assessment 3, Term 4 2024

questions.stem: The shaded region shown, bounded by a chord and the arc it cuts off, is called a:

steps.explain: A segment is the region between a chord and the arc it cuts off. A sector, by contrast, is the "pizza slice" region between two radii and an arc.
steps.work: \text{Region bounded by a CHORD and an arc} \implies \text{segment}

steps.explain: Pitfall: confusing segment with sector (option B) — a sector always has two straight radii as its straight edges, meeting at the centre; a segment has just one straight edge (the chord), which does NOT pass through the centre.

meta.sourcePaper: Hornsby Girls HS — Year 7 Assessment 3, Term 4 2024

questions.stem: A straight line drawn from outside a circle, touching the circle at exactly one point, is called a:

steps.explain: A tangent touches the circle at exactly ONE point and lies entirely outside the circle everywhere else.
steps.work: \text{Line touches the circle at one point only} \implies \text{tangent}

steps.explain: Pitfall: confusing tangent with secant (option B) — a secant is a line that CUTS THROUGH the circle, crossing it at two points, not just touching it at one.

questions.stem: Find the perimeter of the sector shown (radius \(2.1\text{ m}\), sector angle \(306°\)), correct to 1 decimal place.

steps.explain: The perimeter of a sector is made up of two straight radii plus the curved arc. Use the full \(306°\) angle shown (the reflex sector), not the smaller \(54°\) gap.
Substitute \(r=2.1\) and \(\theta=306\).

Pitfall: using the smaller \(54°\) gap instead of the \(306°\) sector shown gives \(6.2\text{ m}\) (option B); forgetting the two straight radii and reporting only the arc length gives \(11.2\text{ m}\) (option C); using the full \(360°\) circumference gives \(17.4\text{ m}\) (option D).

questions.stem: Find the area of the quadrant shown (radius \(6\text{ mm}\)), in exact value.

steps.explain: A quadrant is a quarter of a circle, so its area is \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) of the full circle area.
Simplify, keeping the answer exact (in terms of \(\pi\)) — do not evaluate \(\pi\) as a decimal.
Pitfall: forgetting to divide by 4 (treating it as a full circle) gives \(36\pi\) (option B); dividing by 2 instead of 4 (treating it as a semicircle) gives \(18\pi\) (option C).

questions.stem: The shaded region shown is a semicircle of radius \(3\text{ u}\) with a triangle (base \(3\text{ u}\), height \(2\text{ u}\)) cut out. Find the shaded area, in exact value.

steps.explain: Find the area of the full semicircle first, keeping it exact (in terms of \(\pi\)). The radius is \(3\text{ u}\) — half the full base diameter.
Find the area of the right-angled triangle being cut out, using its base and perpendicular height.

Subtract the triangle from the semicircle. Pitfall: adding instead of subtracting gives \((4.5\pi+3)\) (option B); forgetting the \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) on the semicircle (using the full circle) gives \((9\pi-3)\) (option C); forgetting the \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) on the triangle gives \((4.5\pi-6)\) (option D).

questions.stem: Find the perimeter of a sector with a radius of \(15\text{ cm}\) containing an angle of \(72^\circ\). Give your answer in terms of \(\pi\).
questions.hint: Perimeter of a sector consists of the arc length plus two straight radii. Find the arc length first as a fraction of a full circumference.
questions.solution:
1. A full circle has an angle of \(360^\circ\). The fraction of the circle representing the sector is:
\(\text{Fraction} = \frac{72^\circ}{360^\circ} = \frac{1}{5}\).
2. Find the arc length (\(L\)) of the sector:
\(L = \frac{1}{5} \times 2\pi r = \frac{1}{5} \times 2\pi \times 15 = 6\pi\text{ cm}\).
3. Find the total perimeter (\(P\)) of the sector by adding the arc length and the two bounding radii:
\(P = L + 2r = 6\pi + 2 \times 15 = 6\pi + 30\text{ cm}\).

questions.stem: Find the area of the annulus formed by two concentric circles, one of diameter \(10\text{ m}\) and the other of diameter \(6\text{ m}\). Leave your answer in terms of \(\pi\).
questions.hint: Find the radii of the two concentric circles, calculate their individual areas in terms of \(\pi\), and subtract the smaller area from the larger.
questions.solution:
An annulus is the region between two concentric circles. Its area is \(A = \pi R^2 - \pi r^2 = \pi (R^2 - r^2)\), where \(R\) is the outer radius and \(r\) is the inner radius.
1. Find the outer radius \(R\) from the outer diameter of \(10\text{ m}\):
\(R = \frac{10}{2} = 5\text{ m}\).
2. Find the inner radius \(r\) from the inner diameter of \(6\text{ m}\):
\(r = \frac{6}{2} = 3\text{ m}\).
3. Calculate the area:
\(A = \pi \times 5^2 - \pi \times 3^2 = 25\pi - 9\pi = 16\pi\text{ m}^2\).

questions.stem:
A piece of jewellery is made of two connected circular rings (annuli) as described below:
- The top ring has an outer diameter of \(20\text{ mm}\) and an inner diameter of \(10\text{ mm}\).
- The bottom ring has an outer diameter of \(40\text{ mm}\) and an inner diameter of \(20\text{ mm}\).

Find the total area of plastic needed to make the jewellery, using \(\pi \approx 3.14\).
questions.hint: Find the area of both circular rings (outer area minus inner area) and add them together, using \(3.14\) for \(\pi\).
questions.solution:
1. For the top ring (outer diameter \(20\text{ mm}\), inner diameter \(10\text{ mm}\)):
- Outer radius \(R_1 = 10\text{ mm}\), inner radius \(r_1 = 5\text{ mm}\).
- Area of top ring: \(A_{\text{top}} = \pi(10^2 - 5^2) = 75\pi\text{ mm}^2\).

2. For the bottom ring (outer diameter \(40\text{ mm}\), inner diameter \(20\text{ mm}\)):
- Outer radius \(R_2 = 20\text{ mm}\), inner radius \(r_2 = 10\text{ mm}\).
- Area of bottom ring: \(A_{\text{bottom}} = \pi(20^2 - 10^2) = 300\pi\text{ mm}^2\).

3. Calculate the total area:
- Total Area \(= A_{\text{top}} + A_{\text{bottom}} = 75\pi + 300\pi = 375\pi\text{ mm}^2\).
- Substitute \(\pi \approx 3.14\):
Total Area \(\approx 375 \times 3.14 = 1177.5\text{ mm}^2\).

questions.stem: Clive has a square garden with a side length of \(7\text{ m}\). He designs a vegetable garden with two straight perpendicular paths, each of width \(1\text{ m}\), across the garden. The rest of the garden consists of four symmetric quadrants for vegetable beds, with pavers laid on the remaining paths. What will be the total area of the four vegetable garden beds? Give your answer in square metres, in terms of \(\pi\).
questions.hint: The four quadrants together make up one full circle. Find the radius of one quadrant by subtracting the path width from the side length and dividing by 2.
questions.solution:
1. The square garden has side length \(7\text{ m}\). The perpendicular paths cross through the middle, with a width of \(1\text{ m}\).
2. Subtracting the width of the path (\(1\text{ m}\)) from the total side length (\(7\text{ m}\)) leaves \(6\text{ m}\) for the two opposite quadrant beds.
3. Since the layout is symmetric, each quadrant bed in the corner has a radius of \(r = 6\text{ m} / 2 = 3\text{ m}\).
4. The four corner quadrants together form exactly one full circle of radius \(r = 3\text{ m}\).
5. Total area of the quadrants:
\(\text{Total Area} = 4 \times \left(\frac{1}{4}\pi r^2\right) = \pi r^2 = \pi \times 3^2 = 9\pi\text{ m}^2\).
